case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Fourth Circuit improperly granted federal habeas relief by departing from AEDPA’s exhaustion and deference requirements and by deciding the case on theories allegedly not fairly presented by Sweeney, particularly in connection with juror misconduct/Remmer-type issues and Sixth Amendment fair-trial rights.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2254 (AEDPA), including exhaustion and deferential review; Sixth Amendment right to an impartial jury/fair trial; Remmer v. United States framework for investigating improper juror contacts.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Maryland officials) argue the Fourth Circuit exceeded its authority under AEDPA by (1) excusing exhaustion via a nonstatutory 'special circumstances' exception, (2) effectively reviewing issues de novo rather than applying § 2254(d) deference, and (3) granting relief based on a 'confluence' of constitutional errors and structural-error reasoning that Sweeney allegedly never raised or exhausted in state court or properly presented in federal court—thereby violating the party-presentation principle and creating an ad hoc habeas remedy contrary to Supreme Court precedent.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues summary reversal is unwarranted because the Fourth Circuit’s resolution was not a clear, indisputable departure from settled law; the arguments the Fourth Circuit relied on were in fact raised in Sweeney’s filings and the relevant issues permeated the proceedings; and any mistake would be limited to factbound application (e.g., how juror misconduct and the trial court’s response affected fairness) rather than announcing a broad new legal rule—making this a poor vehicle for extraordinary Supreme Court intervention.
key_precedents: Major League Baseball Players Ass’n v. Garvey, 532 U.S. 504 (2001)
Eaton v. City of Tulsa, 415 U.S. 697 (1974)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point remains that Remmer and Smith v. Phillips demand a meaningful inquiry when there is credible outside influence on a juror, and the state proceedings here may have fallen short in practical effect. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, AEDPA requires us to ask first whether the particular federal theory supporting relief was fairly presented and adjudicated in state court, and then whether the state court unreasonably applied clearly established holdings on that exhausted claim—not a generalized fair-trial principle or a newly minted “confluence”/structural-error framing. Justice Jackson’s Granberry point reinforces that any pre-AEDPA flexibility cannot override § 2254(b)’s “shall not be granted unless” exhaustion command absent a statutory exception or an express waiver, and Sineneng-Smith underscores the institutional problem with the Fourth Circuit supplying its own rationale. A narrow reversal on exhaustion/deference and party-presentation grounds preserves the core Sixth Amendment principle for properly exhausted/direct-review cases without expanding habeas beyond Congress’s constraints.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that Remmer and Smith require a meaningful inquiry into credible external juror influence—does not answer AEDPA’s antecedent textual constraints on federal habeas relief. As Justice Kagan and Chief Justice Roberts emphasize, the Fourth Circuit appears to have reframed the case into a broadened “confluence”/structural-error theory (and perhaps a nonstatutory exhaustion excuse), which cannot be reconciled with § 2254(b)’s categorical exhaustion command and § 2254(d)’s requirement that relief be tethered to an unreasonable application of this Court’s clearly established holdings on the claim actually adjudicated by the state court. Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano confirm that generalized fair-trial principles cannot be transmuted into “clearly established” habeas rules, and Sineneng-Smith underscores the institutional problem when an appellate court supplies its own theory rather than deciding the case the parties and state courts actually litigated. Under a textualist reading of AEDPA, those defects foreclose affirmance even assuming the underlying Sixth Amendment concern is serious.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest opposing point—pressed by Justice Sotomayor—is that Remmer and Smith v. Phillips require a meaningful inquiry into credible allegations of external juror influence, and I agree that interest is substantial on direct review. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, AEDPA imposes threshold, claim-specific constraints: habeas relief must be tied to the exhausted theory actually adjudicated by the state court, and the Fourth Circuit cannot recast the case into a broader “confluence”/structural-error frame or effectively excuse exhaustion outside § 2254(b)’s limited exceptions. Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop confirm that generalized fair-trial concerns cannot be treated as “clearly established” law at a high level of generality to evade § 2254(d) deference, and Sineneng-Smith underscores the institutional problem when an appellate court supplies a new rationale beyond the parties’ presentations. On that statutory and methodological footing, reversal is required even if the state proceeding seemed practically inadequate.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side contention is that Remmer and Smith v. Phillips clearly require a meaningful inquiry once credible external influence on a juror is alleged, and that the state court’s process here was functionally too thin to satisfy the Sixth Amendment. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, AEDPA makes the antecedent questions claim-specific: the federal court must tie relief to the exhausted theory actually presented and adjudicated in state court, and then show an unreasonable application of clearly established holdings to that claim—not a newly supplied “confluence”/structural-error framing. Justice Jackson’s Granberry point matters to my analysis because § 2254(b)’s “shall not be granted unless” exhaustion command leaves little room for nonstatutory bypasses absent waiver or statutory exceptions, and Sineneng-Smith heightens the institutional impropriety of a court of appeals reframing the case. Given Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop’s warning against generalized fair-trial principles on habeas, I think the proper disposition is a narrow reversal enforcing exhaustion/deference, without foreclosing a properly exhausted juror-taint claim on the correct theory.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressed by Justice Sotomayor—is that Remmer and Smith v. Phillips demand a meaningful inquiry when there is credible evidence of external juror influence, and the state proceedings may have fallen short in practical effect. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett correctly re-center that, on habeas, AEDPA requires a claim- and theory-specific inquiry: relief must track what was fairly presented and adjudicated in state court, and then be tied to an unreasonable application of this Court’s holdings on that exhausted claim, not a newly framed “confluence” or structural-error rationale. Justice Jackson’s point about Granberry is decisive for me on exhaustion—whatever flexibility existed pre-AEDPA cannot override § 2254(b)’s “shall not be granted unless” command absent a statutory exception or express waiver, and Sineneng-Smith heightens the institutional problem if the Fourth Circuit supplied its own theory. Under a pragmatic textualist approach, we can preserve Remmer/Phillips as a constitutional baseline while still enforcing AEDPA’s coherent constraints, which means reversal here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressed by Justice Sotomayor—is that Remmer and Smith v. Phillips require a meaningful inquiry into credible allegations of external juror influence, and the state court’s handling may look thin. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, AEDPA’s text demands antecedent, claim-specific discipline: relief must be tied to an exhausted theory actually presented to and adjudicated by the state court, and to an unreasonable application of this Court’s holdings (not a generalized “practical inadequacy” or a reframed confluence/structural-error concept). Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano confirm that habeas courts may not upscale broad fair-trial principles into “clearly established” rules at a high level of generality, and Justice Jackson’s point rightly underscores that Granberry-style flexibility cannot supersede § 2254(b)’s “shall not be granted unless” exhaustion command. On a textualist, separation-of-powers account, the Fourth Circuit’s apparent bypass of exhaustion and party-presentation constraints (Sineneng-Smith) forecloses affirmance even if the underlying Sixth Amendment concerns are serious.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressed by Justice Sotomayor—is that Remmer and Smith v. Phillips require a meaningful inquiry into credible allegations of external juror influence, and the state process here may have been too thin to satisfy the Sixth Amendment on direct review. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, AEDPA demands a claim-specific inquiry tethered to what was actually exhausted and adjudicated, and Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop forbid granting habeas relief based on generalized fairness concerns or a newly reframed “confluence”/structural-error theory. Justice Jackson’s Granberry point reinforces that we cannot invent a nonstatutory exhaustion bypass when § 2254(b) says relief “shall not be granted” absent exhaustion or a statutory exception/waiver. Even accepting the seriousness of the underlying juror-taint allegations, the Fourth Circuit’s approach (as Roberts/Kagan frame it) risks an institutional overstep akin to Sineneng-Smith, so reversal is warranted.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressed by Justice Sotomayor—is that Remmer and Smith v. Phillips require a meaningful inquiry into credible external juror influence, a duty that goes to the core of the Sixth Amendment. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, AEDPA’s text forces claim-specific discipline: habeas relief must rest on an exhausted theory actually presented to and adjudicated by the state court, and then on an unreasonable application of clearly established holdings to that claim—not on a court of appeals’ reframed “confluence”/structural-error rationale. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Granberry underscores that any pre-AEDPA flexibility cannot override § 2254(b)’s “shall not be granted unless” exhaustion command absent a statutory exception or express waiver, and Marshall v. Rodgers/Shoop foreclose using general fair-trial principles to supply the missing clearly established rule. On that statutory and precedential framework, the Fourth Circuit’s approach cannot be sustained even if the underlying Remmer concern is serious.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest opposing-side point, pressed by Justice Sotomayor, is that Remmer and Smith v. Phillips require a meaningful inquiry into credible allegations of external juror influence, and that thin state factfinding can practically obscure Sixth Amendment harm. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, AEDPA compels a claim- and theory-specific threshold inquiry: federal habeas relief must be tethered to the exhausted claim actually presented to and adjudicated by the state court, and the Fourth Circuit cannot evade § 2254(b) and § 2254(d) by invoking a nonstatutory “special circumstances” exhaustion bypass or pivoting to an unpresented “confluence”/structural-error framing. Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop reinforce that we cannot recast generalized fair-trial concerns into a new “clearly established” habeas rule at a high level of generality, and Sineneng-Smith underscores the institutional problem when the court of appeals supplies its own theory rather than deciding the case as litigated. On my pragmatic approach, the proper remedy is to enforce AEDPA’s constraints while leaving Remmer/Phillips to operate fully where the claim is properly preserved and adjudicated on that theory.

John Roberts.reasoning: AEDPA strictly conditions federal habeas relief on proper exhaustion and on deferential review of state-court adjudications, permitting relief only where the state court’s decision is contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law. See 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b), (d). If the Fourth Circuit excused exhaustion through a nonstatutory exception and effectively shifted to de novo review or granted relief on theories not fairly presented, that would conflict with AEDPA’s limits and this Court’s repeated admonitions against lower-court overreach in habeas. See Marshall v. Rodgers, 569 U.S. 58 (2013); Shoop v. Cassano, 142 S. Ct. 2051 (2022). Moreover, deciding the case on unbriefed or recharacterized theories risks violating the party-presentation principle and undermining institutional legitimacy. See United States v. Sineneng-Smith, 590 U.S. 371 (2020).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: AEDPA’s text imposes categorical limits on federal habeas relief: a writ “shall not be granted” unless state remedies are exhausted, except where there is no available state corrective process or it is “ineffective to protect the rights of the applicant,” 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b)(1), and any merits relief must satisfy § 2254(d)’s deferential standards. A federal court may not evade those limits by crafting nonstatutory exhaustion excuses or by effectively reviewing de novo, because § 2254(d) restricts relief to cases where the state court’s adjudication was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law. Nor may an appellate court depart from party presentation and decide a habeas case on theories not fairly presented and exhausted, a concern underscored by Sineneng-Smith and reinforced in habeas by this Court’s repeated admonitions against expanding habeas beyond AEDPA’s commands. Given those constraints, the Fourth Circuit’s reliance on a “special circumstances” path and a confluence/structural-error rationale untethered to exhausted claims is inconsistent with AEDPA and our post-AEDPA precedent enforcing strict deference and narrow grounds for relief.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: AEDPA strictly limits federal habeas relief to claims that were exhausted and then adjudicated unreasonably under clearly established Supreme Court law, and it forbids lower courts from creating equitable workarounds that functionally permit de novo review. See 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b), (d); Shinn v. Ramirez, 596 U.S. 366 (2022). The Fourth Circuit’s approach—excusing exhaustion via a nonstatutory “special circumstances” route and granting relief on a “confluence”/structural-error theory not fairly presented—conflicts with the party-presentation principle and AEDPA’s deference regime. See United States v. Sineneng-Smith, 590 U.S. 371 (2020); Marshall v. Rodgers, 569 U.S. 58 (2013).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Even under AEDPA, federal courts may not ignore exhaustion or § 2254(d) deference, but summary reversal is appropriate only where the court of appeals has plainly flouted clearly established rules, and this record appears factbound and intertwined with the Sixth Amendment’s core guarantee of an impartial jury. Remmer v. United States and Smith v. Phillips establish that credible allegations of external influence on jurors require a meaningful inquiry to protect the fairness of the trial, and the Fourth Circuit could reasonably view the state courts’ handling of juror-contact concerns as constitutionally inadequate in practical effect. While Marshall v. Rodgers cautions that circuit extensions cannot manufacture “clearly established Federal law” for § 2254(d)(1), the gravamen here is the adequacy of the process to test bias—an established principle—rather than a novel categorical rule about every type of misconduct. Given the stakes for a defendant’s fair-trial rights and the absence of an unmistakable AEDPA violation on this procedural posture, I would deny the State’s request to disturb the Fourth Circuit’s grant of relief.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: AEDPA tightly limits federal habeas relief to claims the state courts had a fair opportunity to resolve and to decisions that are contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b), (d). The Fourth Circuit’s apparent move to grant relief based on a broad “confluence” or structural-error framing—especially if that theory was not fairly presented as such in state court—risks evading both exhaustion and § 2254(d) deference, a mistake this Court has repeatedly corrected when courts effectively conduct de novo review (Marshall v. Rodgers; cf. Harrington v. Richter). And to the extent the court of appeals granted relief on grounds not pressed by the parties, that departure from the party-presentation principle conflicts with United States v. Sineneng-Smith and undermines the orderly, workable administration of habeas review. While Remmer supplies an important framework for juror-contact inquiries on direct review, AEDPA requires asking first whether the state court’s handling was unreasonably contrary to clearly established law on the claim actually presented, not whether the federal court would have handled the trial differently.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: AEDPA’s text sharply limits federal habeas relief: a claim must be exhausted absent an express state waiver, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b)(3), and relief may not be granted on any claim adjudicated on the merits unless the state decision was contrary to or an unreasonable application of this Court’s clearly established holdings, § 2254(d)(1), or rested on an unreasonable factual determination, § 2254(d)(2). If the Fourth Circuit excused exhaustion through a nonstatutory “special circumstances” exception and granted relief on a ‘confluence’/structural-error theory not fairly presented and adjudicated in state court, it departed from AEDPA’s commands and from this Court’s repeated admonition that habeas courts may not invent or extend constitutional rules beyond clearly established Supreme Court precedent. Relatedly, deciding the case on theories not presented by the parties would contravene the party-presentation principle recognized in Sineneng-Smith, and the court’s approach would effectively substitute de novo review for § 2254(d)’s “fairminded jurist” deference. Under Shoop v. Cassano and Marshall v. Rodgers, the proper course is reversal where the lower court grants habeas relief without tethering the result to clearly established holdings actually adjudicated under AEDPA’s framework.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: AEDPA sharply limits federal habeas relief to claims that were exhausted in state court and then adjudicated unreasonably under clearly established Supreme Court law, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b)(1), (d)(1), and the Fourth Circuit appears to have relaxed those constraints by excusing exhaustion through a nonstatutory exception and by reframing the case around a cumulative “confluence” theory not fairly presented. That approach risks de facto de novo review and circumvents § 2254(d)’s deference, contrary to this Court’s repeated admonitions that lower courts must not grant habeas relief by expanding the governing legal theory beyond clearly established holdings. Relatedly, deciding on grounds the parties did not squarely present conflicts with the party-presentation principle emphasized in United States v. Sineneng-Smith and with this Court’s AEDPA enforcement in cases like Marshall v. Rodgers. Even assuming Remmer frames how improper juror contacts should be investigated on direct review, AEDPA requires asking whether the state court’s handling was an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law on the claim actually exhausted, not whether the federal court can craft a new aggregate-error rationale.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: AEDPA’s text requires that a federal court deny habeas relief unless the state court’s adjudication was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court precedent, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d), and it separately demands exhaustion of the federal claim in state court, § 2254(b)(1)(A). On this record, the Fourth Circuit appears to have departed from those constraints by effectively excusing exhaustion through a nonstatutory exception and by granting relief on a broadened “confluence”/structural-error theory not fairly presented and adjudicated in state court, in tension with this Court’s insistence on AEDPA deference and methodological discipline. Our cases caution that habeas courts may not reframe claims or supply new legal theories to reach relief (see United States v. Sineneng-Smith, 590 U.S. 371 (2020)) and must anchor relief to clearly established holdings rather than general “fair trial” notions, consistent with Marshall v. Rodgers, 569 U.S. 58 (2013). While Remmer supplies a framework for improper juror contacts on direct review, it does not authorize a federal habeas court to bypass § 2254(b) and (d) or to treat the matter as de novo where the state court addressed the substance of the claim.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: AEDPA makes exhaustion and deference mandatory constraints on granting relief: a writ “shall not be granted unless” state remedies are exhausted or a statutory exception applies, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b)(1), and federal courts may not effectively conduct de novo review when § 2254(d) governs. Granberry v. Greer allowed limited flexibility when the State fails to raise exhaustion and a miscarriage of justice is evident, but it did not authorize a free-floating, nonstatutory “special circumstances” exhaustion bypass—particularly post-AEDPA’s categorical text. The Fourth Circuit’s approach, as described, also raises party-presentation concerns under United States v. Sineneng-Smith by granting relief on a “confluence”/structural-error theory allegedly not fairly presented or exhausted, rather than applying the constrained habeas framework. Given those procedural limits, even serious Remmer-type juror-contact concerns must be assessed through AEDPA’s exhaustion and deference filters rather than by inventing an ad hoc habeas remedy.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Fourth Circuit improperly granted federal habeas relief by departing from AEDPA’s exhaustion and deference rules and by resolving the case on constitutional theories allegedly not presented by the parties, in the context of juror exposure to extraneous information and related ineffective-assistance claims.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2254 (AEDPA)—including exhaustion and deferential review standards (e.g., § 2254(b) exhaustion; § 2254(d) deference); Sixth Amendment right to an impartial jury/fair trial; Sixth Amendment ineffective assistance of counsel doctrine (Strickland framework).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Maryland (Clark et al.) argues the Fourth Circuit flouted AEDPA by (1) excusing or bypassing exhaustion via a vague “special circumstances” theory; (2) failing to apply § 2254(d)’s deferential standard to the only properly exhausted claim; and (3) granting relief based on a “confluence” of alleged constitutional errors—such as an impartial-jury/fair-trial theory and structural-error framing—that Sweeney did not raise in state court, in the district court, or on appeal, thereby violating the party-presentation principle and warranting correction (potentially even by summary reversal). It also argues Supreme Court precedent does not clearly establish that an unauthorized juror crime-scene visit triggers a Remmer hearing, and circuit decisions cannot supply that ‘clearly established’ law under AEDPA.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Sweeney argues summary reversal is inappropriate because the Fourth Circuit’s decision was not a clear, indisputable departure from settled law; the panel relied on arguments Sweeney actually raised (or that permeated the proceedings) rather than inventing new ones; and any missteps would be factbound rather than raising a broad legal question. He also maintains that the jury-taint problem (including the trial court’s and counsel’s failures to determine the scope of prejudice from the juror’s conduct) deprived him of the information necessary to make an informed decision affecting his right to a full jury, and that the lower courts erred in characterizing his filings as only an IAC claim about failing to demand a proper Remmer-type inquiry.

Eaton v. City of Tulsa, 415 U.S. 697 (1974)
Mayhue v. St. Francis Hosp. of Wichita, Inc., 969 F.2d 919 (10th Cir. 1992)
United States v. Perkins, 748 F.2d 1519 (11th Cir. 1984)
United States v. Hillard, 701 F.2d 1052 (2d Cir. 1983)
United States v. Bassler, 651 F.2d 600 (8th Cir. 1981)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that Remmer reflects a baseline duty to conduct a meaningful inquiry into credible external influence, and the state-court record here is thin. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas underscore, AEDPA requires a clearly established holding of this Court that compels the specific hearing/presumption the Fourth Circuit effectively imposed in this distinct posture, and Marshall v. Rodgers bars treating circuit elaborations or “logical next steps” as substitutes for that specificity. Separately, Justice Kagan’s point about the Fourth Circuit’s reliance on a “confluence” of theories not fairly presented or exhausted is dispositive on my minimalist approach: federal habeas relief cannot rest on reframed, unpresented claims without undercutting AEDPA’s channeling function and party presentation (Sineneng-Smith; Wood v. Milyard). The narrow, institutionally legitimate course is reversal on AEDPA/party-presentation grounds while leaving broader Sixth Amendment questions for a case properly postured.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to stress Remmer’s concern with external influence and the need for some meaningful inquiry, but under AEDPA’s text that general "baseline" cannot substitute for a Supreme Court holding that clearly establishes a Remmer-type hearing or prejudice presumption for a juror’s unauthorized crime-scene visit and unclear downstream communications. As Justice Kagan explains, the Fourth Circuit’s reliance on a "confluence" of theories not fairly presented/exhausted compounds the problem because § 2254(b) and the party-presentation principle (Sineneng-Smith) bar federal courts from recasting the claim to evade AEDPA’s channeling function. Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano confirm that habeas courts may not treat logical extensions of our precedents—or circuit refinements of Remmer—as "clearly established" law under § 2254(d)(1). On an originalist and textualist reading of AEDPA, these statutory limits are dispositive, so I would reverse without announcing any broader Sixth Amendment rule on the merits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that Remmer reflects an important Sixth Amendment concern and that an undeveloped record can make prejudice analysis harder, but AEDPA does not ask whether better procedure was advisable—it asks whether the state court unreasonably applied a holding of this Court on these facts. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Marshall v. Rodgers forbids treating Remmer’s general language (or circuit-law elaborations) as “clearly established” law that compels a particular Remmer-type hearing obligation for a juror’s unauthorized scene visit and uncertain communications. Justice Kagan’s point about the Fourth Circuit’s “confluence” rationale reinforces the statutory problem: granting relief on a reframed, not-fairly-presented theory undermines AEDPA’s channeling function and the party-presentation limits reflected in Sineneng-Smith. On my textualist, consequences-attentive approach, reversal on AEDPA/party-presentation grounds remains the legally proper and administrable disposition without expanding juror-taint doctrine on habeas.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s AEDPA/party-presentation concerns seriously, but I do not think they accurately describe what drove relief here: the Fourth Circuit did not need any circuit “refinement” or new “confluence” theory to conclude the state court unreasonably applied clearly established law in refusing to develop the facts underlying a substantial external-influence allegation. Remmer’s core holding is not a high-level aspiration; it is a concrete requirement that credible external contact with jurors be met with a meaningful inquiry adequate to assess prejudice, and the state record’s informational vacuum makes the Strickland prejudice analysis unusually weighty rather than impermissibly speculative. Marshall v. Rodgers properly bars using lower-court extensions as clearly established law, but it does not permit a state court to treat serious juror-taint allegations as effectively harmless while declining to find out what was communicated to the rest of the jury. Sineneng-Smith’s party-presentation principle is a prudential constraint, not a license to ignore that the exhausted ineffective-assistance claim—as actually litigated—necessarily turned on the uninvestigated juror-taint facts that the state court left undeveloped.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that Remmer stands for a meaningful inquiry when there is a credible risk of external influence, and I take seriously her concern about an “informational vacuum” infecting Strickland prejudice. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, AEDPA requires a claim-specific inquiry into whether the state court unreasonably applied a holding of this Court on materially similar facts, and Marshall v. Rodgers/Shoop v. Cassano caution against converting Remmer’s general principle into a new, more specific hearing mandate for juror crime-scene visits and uncertain downstream communications. Separately, the Fourth Circuit’s “confluence” approach looks, as I noted and Justice Barrett underscores, like relief granted on theories not fairly presented or exhausted—an error compounded by the party-presentation constraints reflected in Sineneng-Smith and Wood v. Milyard. On my pragmatic textualist view, the workable and statute-faithful path is reversal on AEDPA channeling/party-presentation grounds without opining broadly on Sixth Amendment merits.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to emphasize Remmer’s general admonition that credible external influence calls for a meaningful inquiry, and I share her concern about deciding prejudice amid an informational vacuum. But AEDPA’s text, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan underscore, asks whether the state court unreasonably applied this Court’s holdings on the claim actually presented and adjudicated—not whether a federal court can extend Remmer’s “core” to a different fact pattern and then treat that extension as clearly established law. Marshall v. Rodgers (noted by Justices Thomas and Barrett) is dispositive on that methodological point: circuit-level elaborations or logical next steps cannot supply the missing specificity under § 2254(d)(1). Add to that the Fourth Circuit’s apparent reframing of the case via unexhausted/party-unpresented theories (Kagan invoking Sineneng-Smith), and reversal follows on narrow statutory grounds without opining broadly on the Sixth Amendment merits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to stress Remmer’s core Sixth Amendment concern: credible external influence should not be waved away without a meaningful inquiry, and an underdeveloped record can complicate Strickland prejudice. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, AEDPA requires a holdings-based, claim-specific analysis, and Marshall v. Rodgers/Shoop v. Cassano forbid treating Remmer’s general language (or circuit “refinements”) as clearly establishing a specific hearing obligation or prejudice presumption for a juror’s unauthorized crime-scene visit and uncertain downstream communications. I also agree with Justice Kagan that the Fourth Circuit’s “confluence” approach appears to grant relief on theories not fairly presented/exhausted, running into § 2254(b) and the party-presentation limits underscored by Sineneng-Smith and Wood v. Milyard. Institutionally, the narrow, legitimate course is to reverse on those statutory/methodological defects without opining broadly on the underlying juror-taint merits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to emphasize Remmer’s “core” insight that credible allegations of external influence warrant a meaningful inquiry, and I share the instinct that an undeveloped record can make prejudice harder to assess. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas stress, AEDPA’s § 2254(d)(1) turns on this Court’s holdings, not general principles abstracted from them, and Marshall v. Rodgers forecloses granting habeas relief by extending Remmer to a distinct setting (a juror’s unauthorized crime-scene visit and uncertain downstream communication) absent a clearly established Supreme Court rule dictating the specific hearing obligation the Fourth Circuit imposed. Justice Kagan’s point about the Fourth Circuit’s “confluence” rationale reinforces that even if Remmer supplies a sensible investigative baseline, habeas relief cannot rest on reframed or unexhausted theories inconsistent with § 2254(b) and the party-presentation limits reflected in Sineneng-Smith. On a textual and precedent-bound reading of AEDPA, those constraints are dispositive here, so I would reverse without reaching broader Sixth Amendment merits.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to stress that Remmer reflects a Sixth Amendment concern with meaningful inquiry into credible external influence, and I share her worry about an “informational vacuum” masking prejudice. But under AEDPA the dispositive question is whether our holdings clearly establish a specific obligation to conduct the kind of Remmer hearing/presumption the Fourth Circuit effectively demanded for a juror’s unauthorized crime-scene visit; as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, Marshall v. Rodgers cautions against converting Remmer’s general principle (or circuit elaborations) into a new, fact-specific rule for § 2254(d)(1). I’m also persuaded by Justice Kagan’s point that the Fourth Circuit’s “confluence” framing looks like a theory shift that strains exhaustion and party presentation (Sineneng-Smith; Wood v. Milyard), which is particularly problematic when it becomes the basis for granting habeas relief. On my pragmatic view, the fair and administrable course is to reverse on these statutory/methodological grounds while leaving room for states to adopt better inquiry practices without federal habeas courts treating them as clearly established constitutional mandates.

John Roberts.reasoning: AEDPA requires exhaustion and imposes deferential review of state-court adjudications on the merits, and a federal habeas court may not grant relief unless the state decision was contrary to or an unreasonable application of this Court’s clearly established holdings. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b), (d). Here, the Fourth Circuit appears to have relaxed those constraints by relying on constitutional theories not fairly presented and by effectively using lower-court extensions of Remmer to supply “clearly established” law, which AEDPA forbids. Marshall v. Rodgers makes clear that circuit precedent cannot "refine or sharpen" our general principles into new specific rules for § 2254(d) purposes, and Sineneng-Smith reinforces that courts should not recast a case on theories the parties did not present. To preserve institutional legitimacy and respect for Congress’s limits on habeas, I would reverse on narrow AEDPA/party-presentation grounds without opining broadly on the underlying juror-taint merits.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: AEDPA’s text requires federal courts to deny habeas relief unless the state-court adjudication was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, “clearly established Federal law, as determined by the Supreme Court of the United States,” 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), and it likewise enforces exhaustion, § 2254(b). The Fourth Circuit erred by effectively relaxing these statutory limits and by relying on a Remmer-type hearing obligation in circumstances this Court has not clearly established—especially where extending Remmer to juror crime-scene visits would be a “logical next step” AEDPA forbids lower courts to take. See Marshall v. Rodgers, 569 U.S. 58, 64 (2013) (per curiam). To the extent the court of appeals granted relief on unexhausted or party-unpresented constitutional theories, that departs from AEDPA’s structure and the party-presentation principle recognized in United States v. Sineneng-Smith, 590 U.S. 371 (2020).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: AEDPA requires strict adherence to exhaustion and deferential review, and a federal court may not grant habeas relief unless the state-court decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b), (d). Here the Fourth Circuit appears to have relaxed those limits and effectively supplied a Remmer-type rule for juror exposure to extraneous information based on circuit extensions, but Marshall v. Rodgers makes clear that circuit precedent cannot "refine or sharpen" Supreme Court doctrine into a new specific rule for AEDPA purposes. The panel also seems to have ventured beyond the parties’ properly presented theories, contrary to the party-presentation principle recognized in Sineneng-Smith, compounding the departure from AEDPA’s framework and risking broad, impractical consequences for finality and law-enforcement interests.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Even under AEDPA’s constraints, the Sixth Amendment’s guarantee of an impartial jury requires a meaningful inquiry when there is a credible showing of external influence on jurors, and Remmer v. United States recognizes that such allegations must be tested in a hearing adequate to determine prejudice. Where the state court and defense counsel failed to develop the basic facts about what the offending juror conveyed to others, the resulting informational vacuum can support Strickland prejudice because it undermines the reliability of the verdict and the defendant’s ability to vindicate his right to a fair jury. Although 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d) demands deference and circuit precedent cannot supply “clearly established” law (Marshall v. Rodgers), the core Remmer principle—investigate substantial external-juror influence rather than presume it harmless—provides enough clearly established baseline to sustain relief on these unusual facts. Given the real-world risk of tainted deliberations and the heightened harm to a defendant who cannot access or test what the jury heard, I would not summarily reverse the Fourth Circuit’s grant of relief.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: AEDPA’s text requires both exhaustion and deference: a federal court may not grant relief on an unexhausted theory absent narrow, recognized exceptions, and it may grant relief on an exhausted claim only if the state court’s adjudication was unreasonable under § 2254(d). On this record, the Fourth Circuit appears to have relaxed exhaustion via an amorphous “special circumstances” rationale and then resolved the case on a “confluence” of constitutional theories not fairly presented, in tension with AEDPA’s channeling function and the party-presentation principle emphasized in Sineneng-Smith. Even if federal courts have some leeway in collateral review to consider forfeited issues, Wood v. Milyard makes clear they lack “carte blanche” to rewrite the case, and Marshall v. Rodgers/ Shoop v. Cassano underscore that circuit authority cannot supply “clearly established Federal law” for § 2254(d) relief. Given AEDPA’s statutory constraints and the apparent mismatch between the theories litigated and the theories used to grant relief, I would vote to reverse.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: AEDPA’s text sharply limits federal habeas relief to claims properly exhausted in state court, and to state-court adjudications that are contrary to or an unreasonable application of this Court’s clearly established law, see 28 U.S.C. §§ 2254(b), (d). The Fourth Circuit’s approach—excusing exhaustion and granting relief on a “confluence” of theories (including impartial-jury/structural-error framings) not fairly presented—conflicts with AEDPA’s party- and claim-specific constraints and the party-presentation principle reflected in Sineneng-Smith. Moreover, under § 2254(d)(1) the court could not treat lower-court extensions of Remmer to non–third-party “extraneous information” as clearly established Supreme Court law, because circuit precedent cannot “refine or sharpen” our general principles into new specific rules for habeas purposes. Given those limits, the Fourth Circuit should have applied § 2254(d)’s deference to the exhausted claim (if any) and denied relief absent a clearly established rule from this Court requiring the particular hearing or presumption it imposed.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: AEDPA tightly cabins federal habeas relief: absent proper exhaustion, a federal court generally may not grant relief, and for claims adjudicated on the merits it must apply § 2254(d)’s highly deferential standard, allowing relief only where the state court unreasonably applied clearly established Supreme Court law. Here, the Fourth Circuit appeared to bypass exhaustion under a judge-made “special circumstances” approach and to grant relief on a “confluence” of trial-error theories not fairly presented by the parties or the state courts, contrary to the party-presentation principle emphasized in Sineneng-Smith and the Court’s repeated insistence that habeas courts not innovate beyond clearly established holdings. Moreover, circuit precedent cannot supply “clearly established Federal law” under § 2254(d)(1), and this Court has cautioned (e.g., Marshall v. Rodgers; Shoop v. Cassano) against using broad generalities to expand habeas relief beyond its statutory limits. Given those constraints and institutional concerns about maintaining AEDPA’s workable, predictable framework, I would vote to reverse the grant of habeas relief.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: AEDPA’s text requires both exhaustion of state remedies, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b), and deferential review of claims “adjudicated on the merits” in state court, § 2254(d), and a federal court may not evade those constraints by reframing the case around unexhausted constitutional theories or a newly minted “confluence” rationale. Under the party-presentation principle, federal courts should not decide cases on theories the parties did not press, see United States v. Sineneng-Smith, and AEDPA likewise bars granting relief based on rules not “clearly established” by this Court. Marshall v. Rodgers makes clear that circuit precedent (or “logical extensions” of Supreme Court doctrine) cannot supply the clearly established law needed to grant habeas relief, undermining any Remmer-based entitlement to relief for a juror’s unauthorized crime-scene visit absent a Supreme Court holding on that specific trigger. Given these constraints, the Fourth Circuit’s approach appears inconsistent with AEDPA’s statutory limits and this Court’s insistence on methodological discipline in federal habeas review.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: AEDPA requires federal courts to respect both exhaustion and the highly deferential standard of review in 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b) and (d), and a court of appeals may not effectively convert an unexhausted or newly reframed “impartial jury/structural error” theory into a grant of § 2254 relief without first ensuring the claim was fairly presented to the state courts. While exhaustion is not “rigid and inflexible” and can yield in “special circumstances,” Frisbie v. Collins and Granberry v. Greer address limited discretion primarily to manage waiver and avoid needless delay—not to supply new merits theories or dilute § 2254(d)’s constraints. The party-presentation principle, as emphasized in United States v. Sineneng-Smith, counsels strongly against appellate courts resolving cases on constitutional rationales not advanced by the litigants, and Wood v. Milyard underscores that any sua sponte intervention must remain bounded and cannot override deliberate litigation choices in a way that changes the case’s theory. Given AEDPA’s structure and the Supreme Court’s repeated admonition that “clearly established Federal law” cannot be supplied by lower-court decisions (see Marshall v. Rodgers), Maryland has the stronger claim that the Fourth Circuit exceeded permissible habeas review if it granted relief on unexhausted, newly minted theories rather than applying § 2254(d) to the exhausted claim.
